articles.title: Building a Quiet Watch Winder: Motor Choice and Killing Resonance
articles.excerpt: I build things for a living, so when my automatic watches started stopping It turned out the mechanical part is trivial. The quiet part is not. A winder's noise budget has three contributors, and they…
articles.body: I build things for a living, so when my automatic watches started stopping over weekends, my first instinct was the obvious one: build a watch winder instead of buying one. How hard can it be? A motor, a cup, a timer. It turned out the mechanical part is trivial. The quiet part is not. Most DIY winders fail on acoustics, not function — they wind fine, and they sound like a small refrigerator compressor parked on your nightstand. Here's what I learned about why they're loud and how to get one under ~30 dB. Where the noise actually comes from A winder's noise budget has three contributors, and they multiply rather than add: Motor and gearbox noise — brushed DC gear motors are cheap and torquey, but the spur gears whine at tooth-mesh frequency.

articles.body: You pulled 250 local businesses into a spreadsheet. Now what? If you call them top to bottom, you spend your best hours of the day on businesses that closed last year, never answer the phone, or are too small to buy anything. A ten-minute scoring pass fixes that. Below is the simple system I use in Google Sheets (Excel works the same way). No add-ons, no paid tools. What you need A lead list with at least these columns. Most directory exports (YellowPages, BBB, Google Maps, Houzz) have them: Business name Phone Address or city Website (can be blank) Rating and review count (if your source has them) Category Years in business or "in business since" (BBB and YellowPages often show this) If a column is missing, just skip that part of the score. The method still works.

articles.title: Embedding Securely: Where the Real Security Boundary Is in ByteChef Embedded
articles.excerpt: You've wired an automation platform into your SaaS: iframes in your UI, signed tokens in the browser, backend API calls, and an MCP endpoint for AI agents. Every one of those is a door into your custo…
articles.body: You've wired an automation platform into your SaaS: iframes in your UI, signed tokens in the browser, backend API calls, and an MCP endpoint for AI agents. Every one of those is a door into your customers' data. So where exactly is the lock? This post walks through the security boundary of ByteChef Embedded and sorts every control into three buckets: what the server enforces , what the UI only hides , and what's left to you . The good news: most of it is on by default. You have two settings to flip and a handful of sample-app shortcuts to fix before real users show up. TL;DR Your backend signs a short-lived RS256 JWT per user. ByteChef verifies it on every request and treats sub as the user. A token works for one user in one environment . Nothing else.

articles.body: "Etsy takes 6.5%" is the most expensive sentence in a seller's vocabulary. 6.5% is real — it's the transaction fee. It's also layer one of five. On a real order, the full stack looks like this (2026 US rates, from Etsy's published Fees & Payments Policy): Fee Rate Transaction fee — on the total the buyer pays, including shipping you charge 6.5% Listing fee — per listing, renewed every 4 months or on each sale $0.20 Etsy Payments processing (US) 3% + $0.25 Regulatory fee 0% US (0.48% UK, up to 1.14% FR) Offsite Ads — only when an ad click drove the order, capped at $100/order 15% (12% if your shop did $10k+ in the last 12 months) The $32 candle, worked by hand Say you sell a candle for $32, charge the buyer $5 shipping, and it costs you $4.60 to ship and $9 in wax, jar and packaging.

articles.title: Your payment webhook will arrive twice. Is your database ready?
articles.excerpt: Every payment provider retries webhooks. If your endpoint is slow, times out, or returns anything other than a 2xx, the provider sends the same event again. Sometimes it sends it again even when you d…
articles.body: Every payment provider retries webhooks. If your endpoint is slow, times out, or returns anything other than a 2xx, the provider sends the same event again. Sometimes it sends it again even when you did everything right, because the response got lost on the way back. So at some point your handler will receive the same payment twice. The usual defence looks like this. if not db . exists ( "SELECT 1 FROM credits WHERE event_id = ?" , event . id ) : db . execute ( "INSERT INTO credits ..." ) It works in every test, and it works in production most of the time. It fails when the two deliveries arrive close together, and then the customer gets paid twice. I wanted to see exactly how that happens, so I reproduced it on a double-entry ledger I've been building in SQL Server.

articles.title: System Design, Plainly — Season 2, Part 7: Gossip Protocols
articles.excerpt: How does a 1,000-node cluster know who's alive? The obvious answer — every node pings every other node — costs about a million messages a round, and it gets worse exactly when the cluster gets bigger.…
articles.body: How does a 1,000-node cluster know who's alive? The obvious answer — every node pings every other node — costs about a million messages a round, and it gets worse exactly when the cluster gets bigger. The answer every real system uses instead is older than the web: gossip. Each node tells a few random peers what it knows, those peers tell a few more, and the whole cluster converges in about seven seconds — at a cost per node that never grows. Cassandra, Consul, and Dynamo all run on it. This is the protocol that makes membership possible at a scale where central registries and all-to-all heartbeats both fall over. The ELI5 version Imagine a rumor in a school of 1,000 kids.

articles.title: Cosmic 'betta fish' glows in spectacular nebula portrait | Space photo of the day for Nov. 26, 2026
articles.excerpt: The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape in a new image from the Dark Energy Camera.
articles.body: An image captured by the Dark Energy Camera showcasing the Betta Fish Nebula. (Image credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA) The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion. What is it? Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape. This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas.
